options: Removes NULL values only
Sorts the results alphabetically
Removes duplicate rows from the result set
Limits the number of rows returned
questions.explain: DISTINCT filters the result set down to unique rows, based on the selected columns.

questions.q: When SELECT DISTINCT includes two columns, what counts as a duplicate?
options: Any row matching on just the first column
Any row matching on just the second column
DISTINCT can only be used with a single column
Rows must match on the entire combination of both columns to be considered duplicates
questions.explain: DISTINCT operates on the whole selected row, not each column independently — Red/Large and Red/Small count as different rows.

questions.q: Why does adding a primary key column to a DISTINCT query usually defeat its purpose?
options: It causes a syntax error
A primary key is unique per row, so every row becomes distinct again, returning all rows
Primary keys can't be selected alongside DISTINCT
It only affects sort order, not row count
questions.explain: Since DISTINCT compares the full row, a column that's already unique (like a primary key) means no two rows can ever match.

questions.q: Where does the DISTINCT keyword go in a SELECT statement?
options: At the very end of the statement
Immediately after FROM
Immediately after SELECT
Inside the WHERE clause
questions.explain: SELECT DISTINCT column_list FROM table — DISTINCT modifies the SELECT clause itself.

questions.q: How does DISTINCT differ conceptually from GROUP BY?
options: GROUP BY can only be used with numeric columns
DISTINCT requires an aggregate function; GROUP BY does not
They are functionally identical in every case
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows; GROUP BY collapses rows into groups for aggregation
questions.explain: They can sometimes look similar in output, but GROUP BY exists to support aggregation (COUNT, SUM, AVG) within groups — covered in Chapter 4.
